newsitem.title: USA: Farm law, synthetics to challenge cotton in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Farm law, synthetics to challenge cotton in 1997.

text.p: Industry members left the annual Beltwide Cotton Conferences for the first time with the knowledge that the new Freedom to Farm law will make their industry a lot more uncertain with the removal of guaranteed government supports.

The 1996 Freedom to Farm Bill, passed last spring, caps federal aid to farmers in exchange for the freedom to plant whichever crops they choose. The previous farm law limited crop acreage but did not impose caps on how much the government could spend to help farmers in times of crisis.

"It all hinges on price," Gaylon Booker, vice president with the National Cotton Council, said. He said that while the industry as a whole supports the flexibility provisions, growers are concerned about the potential for huge financial losses in the event of drought, floods or pest infestation.

"Government before was a stabilizing factor in terms of income," Ronald Knutson, an economist with Texas A&M University, said. "Cotton is subject to more competitive pressures under the 1996 Farm Bill."

Competition will not come from other crops alone this year. With lower production costs and growing capacity in the U.S. and abroad, synthetic fiber is poised to challenge cotton's share of the world fiber market.

"The erratic nature of global cotton production and the increasing competitive nature of man-made fibers, in particular polyester, will continue to encourage the consumption of synthetic fibers at the expense of cotton," Sharon Johnson, an analyst with Frank Schneider and Co Inc, said.

National Cotton Council economist Mark Lange said world polyester use grew 6.8 percent a year between 1990 and 1995, while global cotton demand remained flat. Projections for the next five years place annual world growth in polyester use at seven percent and cotton growth at 1.3 percent.

"Cotton not only faces a challenge to reduce production costs in order to compete with other crops...but if inter-fiber competition is price driven, then lower production costs will be imperative to holding market share in the world fiber market," Lange said.

One way farmers hope to reduce costs is through the use of genetically-engineered Bt cotton. Thousands of members turned out to hear the comments of farmers, cotton specialists, entomologists and industry representatives during a panel discussion on the technology, held earlier this week.
The Bt cottonseed uses the Bacillus thuringiensis gene, which produces a protein that will damage the digestive systems of some pests, thereby reducing farmers' reliance on costly pesticides.

"This is the first time in a long time that something new has helped us stay in the cotton business," Billy Guthrie, a grower from Louisiana, said. "We need to do everything as cheap as possible in order to survive."

In 1996, U.S. cotton farmers planted 1.8 million of a total 14.2 million acres with Monsanto Co's Bollgard cotton, its first year on the market. Despite complaints that the seed did not provide effective control against the bollworm in some areas of the cotton belt, growers said they were anxious to increase Bollgard acreage in 1997 as well as experiment with other genetically-altered products.
A survey released by the St. Louis-based agricultural company found that farmers using the Bollgard technology reported a 7 percent improvement in average yields, compared with other cotton varities.

Monsanto said it will make Bollgard available on a broader basis, and offer its Roundup Ready cotton to growers for the first time, in 1997. Roundup Ready allows farmers to spray crops with herbicides that will kill damaging weeds without harming the cotton plant itself.

"It all begins with the seed," Will McCarty, a cotton specialist with Mississippi State University, said. He said the seed will ultimately deliver insecticides, fungicides, herbicides, and a host of other protective factors, as well as the plant, itself.

But farmers should approach new developments with caution. While transgenic products may manage certain risks, their ability to reduce production costs and increase profits, remains to be seen, McCarty said.
Cotton merchants can look forward to fewer imports in the 1997/98 crop year. As U.S. prices fall more closely in line with world prices, imports are likely to slow, several marketing sources said.

About 4.7 million bales of potential foreign cotton may enter the U.S. under quotas for the past two seasons, but only about 850,000 bales will actually hit U.S. ports, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

"It is my opinion that it is going to be an unusual occurance when volumes of foreign cotton comes into this country as happened last season," leading cotton merchant William B. Dunavant, said. "The American textile industry would much prefer U.S. cotton over foreign cotton and will definitely pay a three to four cent premium."
Last spring, foreign cotton was six to twelve cents cheaper than U.S. cotton, Dunavant said.
